plies to war industries, but the work of the board is closely associated with that of the war-time prices and trade board, the latter board having complete control of prices. Each controller administers the policy of the wartime prices and trade board as applied to the industry over which he exercises control. The following is a brief outline of action taken by the controllers to date:
Machine Tools. Machine tools are basic in war production, and every effort is being made to increase their supply and to restrict their non-essential use. In 1940, designs were frozen on a broad list of consumers' durable goods, including automobiles, in which a change of model would otherwise require new tooling. Every effort has been made to distribute machine tools to war industries in need of such equipment. No exports of machine tools may be made without licence. A government-owned company, Citadel Merchandising Company Limited, assists in the financing of the greatly extended production and purchase of machine tools.
Metals. The metals controller has supervision over the supply, distribution and use of all non-ferrous metals, minerals, and alloys. Substantial restrictions have been imposed on the civilian use of essential metals. In the case of copper, lead and zinc, all tonnage in excess of that required for the Canadian war programme and for greatly restricted domestic requirements is sold under contract to the United Kingdom. The production of metals in Canada has been greatly extended, and this country, which produces the principal base metals such as aluminum, nickel, copper, lead and zinc far in excess of domestic requirements, is supplying these metals in very large quantities to Great Britain and/or the United States of America. In addition, progress has been made in developing sources of strategic metals which were not produced in Canada in any quantity before the war.
In connection with the minerals that are being produced, has any plant in Canada yet come into the production of magnesium metal?
The first magnesium metal from a pilot plant is being produced now. We have not undertaken large-scale development.
Where is the pilot plant?
I think it is here in Ottawa, at the research laboratories.
There is one small plant in Hamilton, I believe.

I do not think that one is in operation.

Mercury has been in production for over a year, and tungsten, antimony and manganese are being developed.
Motor Vehicles. The motor vehicle controller has substantially reduced the number of passenger cars which may be manufactured in Canada in order that materials and labour may be directed to the manufacture of war vehicles. For 1942 the rate of production of passenger cars has been established at 44 per cent of 1940 production, which is the equivalent of 50 per cent of 1941 production. Steps have been taken to spread this reduced output evenly through the year, to avoid unnecessary peaks and valleys in labour and material requirements.
Oil. A number of orders have been issued by the controller to restrict civilian use of gasoline. These include reduction of deliveries to service stations to 80 per cent of estimated normal requirements, and prohibition of the erection of new service stations, gasoline pumps, storage tanks and oil-burning equipment. Sale of gasoline and oil to motorists on Sundays and at night (from 7 p.m. to 7 a.m.) on week days has been prohibited. Grades of gasoline for public use are limited to two, and credit cards may no longer be used by Canadians. Voluntary cooperation in saving gasoline has been requested, and a list of pointers on how to save gasoline and oil has been placed before the public.

construction of new buildings costing more than $10,000, installation of equipment costing more than $5,000, and making repairs in excess of $2,500 are all subject to licence of the construction controller. (a)	Silk. (d)	Transparent film. The .use of transparent films of the "cellophane" variety has been substantially curtailed, and with certain specific exceptions is limited to use as cellulose adhesive tape and for packaging food, candy, drugs and tobaccos when not in tin or glass containers.

The general principle underlying the curtailment measures is that monthly production for the time being is to be reduced to 75 per cent of 1940 monthly average output. Committees of representatives of the industries concerned are being formed to assist in the efficient and equitable application of this principle.

Power. In order to ensure adequate supplies of power for war industries, the power controller has instituted daylight saving applicable throughout the year in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec in the case of those communities which observed daylight saving in the summer of 1940. Use of electric power for steam purposes has been banned and coal boiler installations made, making such power available for war industry. Certain non-war industries have been forced to reduce consumption of power during peak hours. In central areas all power systems have been inter-connected, so as to permit excess power in one area of the country to be used in other areas as required. Many improvements in plants have been arranged on the order of the controller to ensure maximum production of power from all capacity.
I have endeavoured to give hon. members the highlights of Canada's munitions programme without undue detail, but, even so, it has been a long story. I feel that the men and women of Canada are beginning to understand the all-out nature of our productive effort. Looking back over the past two years, I do not see. how our full production could have been developed any more rapidly than it is being developed. I have been supported by the unfailing devotion to duty of a very able, staff drawn from Canadian industry, and I have also had the fullest cooperation from Canadian manufacturers and from Canadian workmen. Canada's position in war production will stand comparison with that of any country in the world, and recent comparisons that have been made by competent observers are highly complimentary to this country. Our war industries are soundly established, and our present production is all that, and in many cases more than, we had anticipated. It has been our purpose to call on Canadian industry and Canadian man-power for the maximum that the most optimistic estimates of capacity would permit. While we believe that we are reaching the end of possible productive capacity, we are still taking on new projects to the extent that further possible productive capacity can be discovered. If, in the past, other countries have looked upon Canada as a source of raw materials rather than of finished products, the future will find us a country equipped to turn our own raw materials into finished products within our own borders.
It has been our purpose in planning our war industries to maintain a balance between available supplies of raw material and our planned war production. We have counted on curtailment of domestic production of a non-essential character and this is now being

The War-Naval Services-Mr. Macdonald
brought about through our controllers. I wish to assure hon. members that the only purpose of curtailing of domestic articles is to free necessary raw materials for our munitions programme and to provide needed manpower for that programme. We will continue to make available for domestic use everything not absolutely required by the war programme, and we will not call upon our people for sacrifices that are not entirely necessary to bring about the success of our war effort.
Such measures of restriction as have already been applied have, in general, obtained the full cooperation of our citizens. I ask all hon. members to cooperate with our controllers in explaining to our citizens the need for restriction and in asking for cooperation.
There is no reason to believe that this war will end in the near future. Our industrial effort must foe sustained over a long period. We have planned with this in view. Munitions from Canada are now reaching every theatre of war in quantities that are impressive to those receiving them. We have established a reputation of quality and prompt delivery. There is an enthusiasm behind our production that is accomplishing results greater in many cases than we had hoped for. I am confident that, in the months to come, Canada will make history as an industrial nation engaged ' in an all-out effort in war production.

MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services): Mr. Chairman, it is now nearly a year since I gave to the house what I then endeavoured to make a comprehensive review of the strength, work, and prospects of the Royal Canadian Navy. In the course of the year that has passed there have been discussions on naval matters both in the house and in committee, but no general statement on the Royal Canadian Navy was made in that period. I shall endeavour now to give briefly and simply some further account of our naval effort during the past year.
When I spoke a year ago I was able to tell the house that the Canadian navy had increased from a strength of 1,774 officers and men on active service at the beginning of the war to a strength of 13,000 officers and men on active service in November, 1940. Those figures represented an eight-fold increase in the space of fourteen months. I stated then that we planned to have 23,000 men and 250 ships by March 31, 1942. I am happy to be able to say that now, six months before that date, we have considerably exceeded that estimate. In the last twelve months the increase in personnel has been even greater than during the first fourteen months of the war. The total strength of
the Royal Canadian Navy to-day is 27,000 officers and men, a truly phenomenal expansion from the first days of the war. What is more, there is no dearth of recruits; there is no lack of men offering to serve in the navy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services

- that there is no dearth of men. Men are being taken into the naval service as rapidly as they can be trained and as rapidly as ships can be provided for them. You cannot train naval officers particularly, and petty officers, in a short time, but they are being trained as rapidly as is possible in this country and England, and as soon as they are trained there is a place for them.
As to where these men serve I may say to the hon. member for Davenport that they are to be found in every sea of the world. The great majority of them, of course, are to be found in Canadian ships but several hundred of them have been lent to the Royal Navy. These men of the Canadian navy who are serving with the Royal Navy are paid by Canada and at Canadian rates of pay.
To turn now to the question of ships, it is to be noted that the increase here has kept pace almost exactly with the increase in personnel. A year ago the number of ships in the Canadian navy was 155. The number to-day is 300. In that number are included auxiliary cruisers, destroyers, corvettes, minesweepers, patrol boats and auxiliary vessels of a great variety of types.

The War-Naval Services-Mr. Macdonald
Like the men of the Canadian navy, our ships are to be found in widely scattered parts of the world. One cannot, of course, specify with definiteness where the ships are at a given time, but it may be said without fear of betraying any secrets that at this moment Canadian ships are separated by 10,000 miles of land and sea. Some of them are on convoy work; some are protecting the shores of this country, and still others are cooperating with the royal navy. The work of convoying both freight ships and troop ships still continues to be one of the most important tasks of the Canadian navy. How important is this work to the success of our cause, and how vital it is to the very life of the British isles are matters that are beyond dispute. It is a source of gratification to be able to say that not one ship proceeding in troop convoy from these shores to Great Britain has lost a single passenger on the way. So far as freight convoys are concerned no fewer than 7,000 ships have left Canadian shores for Great Britain since the outbreak of the war, carrying 42,500,000 tons of cargo to that island. A great deal of the work of convoying these ships and their cargoes has fallen to the Canadian navy. I shall not attempt to specify how this work is allotted, where the duty of one service ends and another begins, but it is true to say that a great part of it, and a very hazardous part, falls to the care of the men of the Canadian navy.
We have been greatly heartened, and I believe that the whole empire has been cheered by certain steps taken not long since by the navy of the United States. The great president of that great country has indicated clearly that certain portions of the seas which lie between America and Europe and which he regards as of primary importance to United States security will be patrolled by United States ships of war. He has asserted the principle of the freedom of the seas in those areas, and the ships of the United States navy are now defending that principle. The decision of the United States president is one of great importance and of great assistance to us and to our cause.
On more than one occasion the work of the Canadian navy has won the commendation of naval authorities in other countries. Thus, speaking in Bermuda in September last, Mr. Frank Knox, Secretary of the Navy of the United States, said that the Canadian navy is doing, to quote his exact words, "a very outstanding job" in the defence of north American sea approaches, and he added that it had been "a very considerable help to the whole problem of transport".

Writing in the Fortnightly Review for September of this year, Admiral Sir Henry Richmond, in an article entitled "The War at Sea" uses the following words in speaking of the need of increasing the strength of escort forces:
The prospects of such strengthening are encouraged by the news from Canada of the truly remarkable developments of the Royal Canadian Navy. Canada, who began the war with a diminutive navy of thirteen small vessels and 1,774 officers and men, now commands the services of 250 vessels and a personnel of 22,000, and these are employed as far afield as the Caribbean sea, the north Atlantic and the European waters. Besides this, her shipbuilding programme has included the construction of no less than seventy of those useful little vessels, the corvettes, of which sixty were for the Canadian and ten for the British navy, sixty mine-sweepers and a large number of other small craft. Nor is this all that she has contributed to the defence at sea. Her troops have furnished reinforcements for the defence of Iceland, Newfoundland and the West Indies, and her forty shipbuilding and repairing yards are producing merchant ships. These are efforts which should not go unnoticed in this country; they are harbingers of even greater things and they show the awakening of the maritime spirit of that great dominion.
Those are the words of Admiral Sir Henry Richmond. These are significant statements. But added proof can be presented of the value of the work that has been done by Canadian naval forces. Such proof is to be found in the awards and mentions for gallantry. On no fewer than forty-nine occasions, officers and men of the Royal Canadian Navy have received decorations, mentions in dispatches, or commendations for their performances. This alone is proof of the valour of our Canadian naval personnel and of the importance of the work which they are doing.
This work is not carried on without its casualties. Since the beginning of the war 364 officers and men have been killed, sixty-seven have been wounded and two are prisoners of war. In the last year two ships of the Canadian navy have been lost. One the Otter an armed patrol ship, caught fire and foundered off Halifax in March of this year with a loss of nineteen men. More recently the corvette Levis, while escorting a convoy, was torpedoed with a loss of seventeen men.
But we have something to show on the other side of the ledger. We, too, have taken our toll. Five enemy merchant ships have been captured by our navy since the commencement of hostilities. Enemy submarines have been frequently attacked by our ships, mainly by depth charges, and while it is not possible or proper to give the details of these actions, it may be said with certainty that some of the attacks have been completely successful and that more than one German

The War-War Services-Mr. Thorson
U-boat now lies at the bottom of the sea as a result of the vigilance and skill of men of the Canadian navy.
The protection of merchant shipping is one of our tasks, but the provision of merchant ships and of merchant seamen is in other hands. The Canadian naval staff, however, have taken a deep interest in the training and supply of merchant seamen and have cooperated with the Department of Transport in the provision of manning pools in this country, where merchant seamen may register and remain while awaiting employment on a merchant ship.
Two hundred ratings of the Royal Canadian Navy are now serving as gunners or in some similar capacity on defensively equipped merchant ships.
There are two other matters which I should like to mention briefly in this statement. The first is that very shortly we hope to begin the building of destroyers in this country. Already some skilled naval constructors from England have arrived to supervise this work. Plans for destroyers are well in hand, and as soon as material is available-and this will be on hand very shortly-the work of destroyer-building in Canada will commence.
The second matter which I wish to mention is that we hope to open the Royal Canadian Naval College in the autumn of 1942. This college will be a training ground for officers of the navy, and I believe it will prove to be an invaluable addition to our programme of organizing the Canadian navy.
Expansion in ships and men of the Canadian navy has been substantial, but we aim at still further expansion. We shall have more men and more ships. Changes being made in the art and the practice of naval warfare require changes in ship construction and in the training of naval personnel. We are endeavouring to the utmost of our ability to keep in touch with the latest improvements in training and in shipbuilding and in ship armaments.
The work of the empire navies in this war is of prime and overriding importance. The task of carrying supplies overseas and of protecting the ships wliich carry those supplies is one which need take second place to none other in the strategy of this war. We must have more merchant ships to replace those that are lost, and to do more than replace them, to make the merchant navies of the empire larger and more efficient than they were before. But merchant navies without the protection of fighting ships are helpless to-day. More and more this fact is being emphasized. Greater and greater becomes the need for more and better escort vessels. Our shipyards in Canada, under the direction of the Minister
of Munitions and Supply, have done magnificently up to the present. They will continue, I know, their splendid record.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I think I can say with modesty that the personnel of our navy has brought honour to itself and to this country. It will be the aim of the department of naval services to continue to improve upon the work of the past and to spare no effort of thought or labour in carrying out its duties, which are so vital to the successful prosecution of this war.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. T. THORSON (Minister of National War Services):
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Department of National Defence for Naval Services has under its charge the drama of the navy. The department over which I have the honour to preside has no such drama. Many of its activities are of a prosaic nature, but they are nevertheless important. A number of functions have been assigned to the Department of National War Services. The department, since the house last adjourned, has been reorganized to a certain extent. This afternoon I tabled an order in council, P.C. 8488, dated the 31st day of October, 1941. This order in council authorizes certain divisions of the department and sets out the purposes of such divisions. It indicates the great variety of the functions that are assigned to this department.
Perhaps I could best illustrate this diversity by reading the operative parts of the order in council:
The following divisions of the Department of National War Services are hereby authorized for the purposes hereinafter set forth:
(a) The National Registration division-to administer and carry out the national registration regulations, to record and tabulate new registrations, to record changes of address and of matrimonal status, to compile statistical and such other information as may be required as a result of the said national registration, and to prepare lists of men as may be required under the national war services regulations or otherwise.
The national registration which took place in August, 1940, was the first task assigned to the new department that was created on July 12, 1940. While the employees of the national registration division are on the staff of the department, they act under the supervision of the dominion bureau of statistics. Many of the results of the national registration are to be found in a number of publications, issued by the Department of National War Services in conjunction with the dominion bureau of statistics. The first of these is the preliminary statistical tabulation of the national registration of August, 1940. Then there is the table of specialized occupations, also issued by the
4094	COMMONS
The War-War Services-Mr. Thorson
Department of National War Services and the dominion bureau of statistics. And finally, statistics relating to labour supply under war conditions, issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, dominion bureau of statistics, social analysis branch.
The second division that is authorized is called the mobilization division. Its functions are:
To administer and carry out the national war services regulations, and to direct the mobilization of men for military training under the said regulations, of women volunteers for auxiliary service with the army, navy or air force, as requisitioned from time to time, of fire-fighters for service in the United Kingdom, and of such other persons as may be required from time to time; to keep the records of the voluntary service registration bureau, and to assist in directing those seeking war employment to employment and towards training facilities which may be available; to give information and other services in connection with prisoners of war and Canadian internees in enemy occupied countries.
The next division referred to in the order in council is that of public information. Its purposes are;
To direct the activities of the bureau of public information; to collect and disseminate to the public information concerning the various phases of the war effort of the Canadian people and the activities of the government in relation thereto; and, generally, to coordinate the existing public information services of the government and originate or employ other means in order that the same may be [DOT]used in the most efficient way for the obtaining of the utmost aid from the people of Canada in the national emergency which has arisen.
I like to think of the functions of the public information bureau as being carried out with one objective, to bring the war effort of this country as close to the hearts and minds of the people of Canada, and the people of Canada as close to our war effort, as it is possible to do. Indeed I conceive that to be perhaps the main objective of the department which has been placed under my charge.
The Minister of National Defence some time ago spoke of four things as being necessary for the successful prosecution of the war: men, munitions, money and morale. I hope that the department over which I preside may make some contribution towards keeping the morale of the country at its highest possible level.
The next division referred to in the order in council is the war charities division. The purpose of this division is:
To administer The War Charities Act and the regulations made thereunder, to cooperate with all organizations registered under The

War Charities Act, including such organizations as are or may become subject to the supervision of the national war charities funds advisory board, and generally to promote, organize and coordinate different forms of voluntary assistance with a view to the most effective use of personal services or material contributions for the prosecution of the war and the welfare of the nation.
The next division that I shall refer to is the women's voluntary services division. This is a new division of the department, and I am very happy indeed to be able this evening to announce its creation. The purpose of this division is:
To promote the coordination of the voluntary efforts of the women of Canada and to encourage the organization of women's voluntary services on a community basis, with a view to their best utilization for the needs of their communities, the maintenance of national morale and the furtherance of the welfare of the nation.
Then there is another division that is called the salvage division, of which the purposes are:
To strengthen the spirit of thrift in the minds of the people of Canada; to encourage the conservation of raw materials and promote the salvage, collection and disposal of secondary raw materials; to direct and supervise the organization of voluntary salvage corps; to cooperate with other departments concerned with the conservation and use of secondary raw materials and assist in the making of the necessary arrangements between producers, dealers and consumers, and to prepare information for distribution.
These are the functions of the department which are authorized by the order in council.
Then certain statutory functions have been assigned to me. One of them is the supervision of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation so far as broadcasting is concerned; another is the chairmanship of the national film board of which I shall speak later. Then further the administration of the Canadian travel bureau has been assigned to my department, and I have been asked to assist in the coordination of censorship activities throughout the various departments of the government.
I shall not attempt to speak of these various functions at any appreciable length. I shall not deal with the national registration or the manner in which that was carried out; that was very fully covered by my predecessor when he spoke earlier this year.
But I should like to say just a few words about the various functions of the mobilization division. The first of these functions has to do with the calling up of men for military training in accordance with the provisions of the national war services regulations made and established in virtue of the National Resources Mobilization Act and the War Measures Act.

The War-War Services-Mr. Thorson
As all hon. members are aware, the national war services regulations provide that every male British subject who has been at any time subsequently to the first day of September, 1939, ordinarily resident in Canada, while (as of July 1, 1940) of the ages of twenty-one to forty-five years inclusive and unmarried or a childless widower is liable during the continuation of the state of war now existing to undergo military training for such period as the governor in council may determine by proclamation. On or about the 1st day of July of this year men of the age classes of 21, 22, 23 and 24 as of July 1, 1940, and men as they become 21 years of age subsequently to that date, have been called out by proclamation. (The date of the proclamation as given, July 1, 1940, is not perhaps the correct date, but I have not the exact date now before me). The provisions of the national war services regulations are administered by thirteen administrative divisions established, roughly corresponding to the military districts of Canada. In each one of these divisions there is a board consisting of a chairman and two other members. The chairman of each board is a judge of a superior court or other court of the province in which the administrative division is located. The other two members are prominent and respected citizens of the community. In addition, authority to appear before the board at its hearings is given to a representative of the Department of National Defence and to a representative of the national labour supply council. The various national war services boards are completely in control of the administration of the regulations, and their decisions in all of the matters that come before them are final and conclusive. The Department of National War Services in Canada therefore does not deal with individual cases.
Would the minister explain how those hockey players got out of the country?
I shall be glad to deal with that when we are in discussion.

I should not like the minister to forget it.
Mr.' THORSON:	The department in
Ottawa does not deal with any individual cases. If the hon. leader of the opposition suggests that the departure of the hockey players was a result of any intervention on the part of the department in Ottawa I can inform him that he is entirely mistaken.
I do not say anything of the sort, but I want to know how these young men got out of the country when they were subject to military draft.

I shall deal with that subject when we come to discussion. All communications concerning any young men who are called out for military training should therefore be addressed to the registrar of the administrative division in which the man concerned resides.
Roughly, the purposes of the Department of National War Services in respect of the calling out of men for military training are these: The Department of National Defence indicates from time to time, usually monthly, the number of men that the department requires for military training. A requisition setting this out is sent to the Department of National War Services, and on receipt of instructions to that effect each divisional registrar selects the young men and sends them notices to appear before any medical practitioner in good standing. The men are selected by the divisional registrars from the several cities, towns, villages and the countryside, so that all portions of the division shall furnish men in as equitable a manner as possible.
By what method does 'he select them? I know the practice, but what is the method of selection?
The selection is by age groups; first the twenty-ones, then the twenty-twos, and so on.
Has the registrar any right to say this man shall go and that man shall not go?

He has assigned to him the duty of selecting men from the province or administrative division over which he has jurisdiction. I should like to deal more specifically with the question raised by my hon. friend when we get into the discussion.
Did I understand the minister to say that a young man who is called up has the right to appear before any qualified medical practitioner?

Yes, in the first instance, since all medical practitioners in good standing have been appointed examining physicians by the Department of National War Services. Therefore in the first instance a man may go to any doctor of his own choice. Then the medical certificates that come in from these practitioners are subject to scrutiny in the department. These medical practitioners examine the men in accordance with the physical standards for the examination of recruits as laid down by the Department of National Defence. The men who are found physically fit for training are then notified
4096	COMMONS
The War-War Services-Mr. Thorson
to report at an indicated training centre of the Department of National Defence, where they undergo four months' training.

May I just interrupt to ask whether this is the final medical examination? Are those reported fit accepted on the strength of that certificate, or do they undergo another medical examination when they report at the training centres?
I do not think they do.
Yes, they do.
I think the minister should inform himself on that point.

Once the men have been delivered to the training centre they come under the jurisdiction of the Department of National Defence and are no longer subject to the jurisdiction of the Department of National War Services. There has been a misunderstanding of the situation with regard to this military training.

Before he leaves this question of the medical examination, would the minister take steps to inform himself not only with respect to the matter to which I alluded but also with regard to this situation? Young men go to their own family physicians and are reported unfit for service; is there any review of those cases?
Yes.	,
I should like to have that made quite clear.
Yes, those cases are also subject to review by medical examiners of the department in the various divisions, who check up the rejections.
I should like to know how many rejections have been checked during the year or so this plan has been in operation.

I shall be glad to give full particulars in that regard.
I was dealing with the subject of the four months' training. The men are called up for this training under the provisions of a proclamation issued through my department. When they are delivered to the training centre they become subject to the Department of National Defence, which department has issued orders, which are now routine orders, holding these men in continuous service for the duration of the war. I am happy to say that the requisitions of the Department of National Defence have been filled by the Department of National War Services without any difficulties whatever. I should like to pay a tribute to the youth of Canada,
fMi. Thorson.]
to their parents and their friends, for the manner in which they have come forward, willingly and freely, for this compulsory military training-
Have they any alternative?
-as men who realize the vital and pressing need of preparing themselves for the defence of their country.
Might I ask the minister if they have any alternative?
Perhaps not, but I am commenting upon the splendid manner in which they have responded, and I should like to pay tribute to them. There have been very few delinquents indeed.
Could the minister give us the number of delinquents?

I think I can get that information for my hon. friend. The National War Services regulations contain special provisions that are designed to facilitate equitable conditions of mobilization. If the board is satisfied, for example, that the calling out of a man for military training will cause extreme hardship to his dependents, the board may postpone the training period of such man, provided that he applies for a postponement order in accordance with the regulations. Special consideration is also given, in accordance with the regulations, to employees of war industries and men engaged in seasonal occupations and in activities essential to the successful prosecution of the war. But I should remind hon. members that there are no exemptions, and that there are no indefinite postponements.
I should like to correct the minister's statement. He has said that there are no exemptions, but he must admit that there are exemptions from military service for Doukhobors and Mennonites.
And conscientious objectors.

There are some persons who are excepted from the application of the regulations, but they are very limited in number. Those persons are set out in section 6 of the regulations, and include judges, members of the clergy, members of the naval, military or air forces, and the like. But those are classes that are excepted from the application of the regulations. I repeat that in respect of those subject to the regulations there are no exemptions and no indefinite postponements.

Would the minister mind stating for how long the postponements

Questions
are granted? For instance, what is the limit in respect of the postponement a young man operating a farm or business might receive?

Usually postponements
do not exceed six months at any one time.

The department ought to be abolished; it helps Hitler more than Canada.
